idiom_name: weak (and unowned where liveness is guaranteed) under ARC; [weak self] capture lists; a Weak<T> box or NSHashTable for collections
implementation_notes: Swift is the pattern at language level: ARC tracks strong references, and weak on a class-typed property or variable creates an edge that does not keep the instance alive and is automatically set to nil when the instance is deallocated - which is why a weak reference must be var and Optional, and why the promotion is simply optional binding (if let target = ref). unowned is the sibling strength for references that are guaranteed to outlive their holder: it is non-optional and traps if the instance is gone, so it is not a weak reference in this pattern's sense. Capture lists ([weak self], [unowned self]) apply the same choice to closures, which is the standard fix for object-closure retain cycles. The standard library has no weak collection, so a weak registry uses a small Weak<T> box (a class with a weak var) or Foundation's NSHashTable.weakObjects().
pitfalls: A weak property must be of class type, declared var and Optional: structs, enums and let constants cannot be weak, and the compiler rejects the attempt.
unowned assumes the referent never dies and traps at runtime when it does - choosing it to avoid optionals turns a tolerated absence into a crash.
A closure that captures self strongly forms a retain cycle; [weak self] makes self optional inside the closure, and the guard/unwrap is the promotion step - forgetting it defeats the weak capture.
No weak collections exist in the standard library: an array of weak elements needs the Weak<T> box or NSHashTable.weakObjects(), and the structure must reap nil entries itself.
